Context/Background:
Intraductal papillary neoplasms (IPNs),  including intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasms (IOPNs), and intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasms (ITPNs), are clinically detectable macroscopic non-invasive cyst-forming lesions, some of which progress to invasive pancreatic cancer. Proteins and glycoproteins have proven to be useful clinical biomarkers for classifying cyst-forming neoplasms in the pancreas.Here, we used proteomics and glycoproteomics to characterize a series of histologically and genetically well-characterized surgically resected IPNs, including IPMNs and IOPNs.

Our analysis included 69 IPNs (64 IPMNs and 5 IOPNs), 76 macro-dissected grossly normal duct tissues (NDs, with 32 of the 76 NDs coming from the same resection specimens as the IPNs), and 32 cyst fluid samples (22 from matched IPMN patients, 3 matched IOPN patients, 2 from unrelated IPMN patients, and 5 other cysts).
Prompt: Compare the differential genes on global proteome level and glycoproteome level for IPMN vs ND.  Provide a pathway level summary of biological functions of upregulated or downregulated glycopeptides whose global protein expression remained unchanged.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
We compared global‐proteome (Table S2A; 9 417 UniProt entries quantified) and glycoproteome (Table S3I; 85 glycopeptides) profiles of IPMN versus adjacent normal duct (ND) tissues from surgically resected specimens. At the proteome level, most of the measured proteins (e.g., carboxypeptidases, receptor tyrosine kinases, adhesion molecules) showed either small fold‐changes or did not reach FDR < 0.05 significance (“not specified” for replicate number and other metadata). In the glycoproteome, 77 glycopeptides were significantly upregulated and 1 downregulated (FDR < 0.05). By intersecting these lists, we identified a subset of glycopeptides whose parent protein abundance remained statistically unchanged (prot_FDR ≥ 0.05): seven glycopeptides from carboxypeptidase D (CPD; all up) and one from TLR8 (down).

Keywords  
• Glycosylation • Vesicle trafficking • Proteolysis • Innate immunity • Rho GTPase

Candidate Genes  
CPD | TLR8 | ADAM10 | MET | ERBB3

Pathway Enrichments (ORA on upregulated glycopeptides with unchanged protein abundance)  
Reactome_Pathways_2024 (UP):  
| Theme                                     | Direction | Leading Genes |  
|-------------------------------------------|-----------|---------------|  
| RND1 GTPase Cycle                         | Up        | CPD           |  
| RND3 GTPase Cycle                         | Up        | CPD           |  
| trans-Golgi Network Vesicle Budding       | Up        | CPD           |  
| Golgi Associated Vesicle Biogenesis       | Up        | CPD           |  
| Membrane Trafficking                      | Up        | CPD           |  
| Vesicle-mediated Transport                | Up        | CPD           |  
| RHO GTPase Cycle                          | Up        | CPD           |  
| Signaling by Rho GTPases                  | Up        | CPD           |  

GO_Biological_Process_2023 (UP):  
| Theme                         | Direction | Leading Genes |  
|-------------------------------|-----------|---------------|  
| Peptide Metabolic Process     | Up        | CPD           |  
| Protein Maturation            | Up        | CPD           |  
| Protein Processing            | Up        | CPD           |  
| Proteolysis                   | Up        | CPD           |  

Analysis  
Carboxypeptidase D (CPD) glycopeptides are consistently upregulated (log₂FC 0.96–2.51; FDR < 0.05) despite unchanged total CPD protein (prot_FDR = 0.109). ORA highlights CPD’s involvement in Rho-GTPase–mediated vesicle budding at the trans-Golgi network and broad membrane trafficking, alongside its core role in peptide maturation and proteolysis. This suggests that altered N-glycosylation of CPD may fine-tune its trafficking through Golgi compartments and its enzymatic activity without changing overall abundance. In contrast, TLR8 shows a single downregulated glycopeptide (log₂FC –0.78; FDR = 0.0468) with undetectable change at the protein level, implicating potential dampening of innate immune receptor glycosylation.

Targeted Subset (keyword‐guided filtering)  
Filtering ORA terms by “vesicle,” “peptid,” “GTPase” confirmed enrichment of CPD in RND/RHO GTPase cycles, vesicle biogenesis, trans-Golgi network budding, and proteolytic processes. No direct Reactome or GO terms emerged for TLR8 from single‐gene ORA; however, TLR8’s established function in endosomal pathogen sensing (TLR signaling) aligns with its downregulated glycosylation.

Key Genes/Proteins (leading‐edge)  
Upregulated glycopeptides with unchanged protein:  
| Gene | Direction | Role/Function                         | Pathway(s)                                                     |  
|------|-----------|---------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|  
| CPD  | Up        | Metallocarboxypeptidase; peptide maturation | RND1/RND3 GTPase Cycle; trans-Golgi vesicle budding; Proteolysis |  

Downregulated glycopeptides with unchanged protein:  
| Gene | Direction | Role/Function                                       | Pathway(s)               |  
|------|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------|--------------------------|  
| TLR8 | Down      | Endosomal Toll-like receptor; innate immune sensor  | TLR signaling (inferred) |

Comparisons  
• Only CPD and TLR8 exhibited significant glycosylation changes without corresponding protein‐level shifts, highlighting post-translational rather than transcriptional or translational regulation.  
• CPD glyco-up signatures point to enhanced Golgi‐mediated trafficking and protein processing in IPMNs, whereas down-glycosylation of TLR8 may attenuate ductal innate immune sensing.  
• Other glycoproteins (ADAM10, MET, F3, ERBB3) showed concordant protein and glyco abundance changes and were excluded here.

Implications  
Altered CPD glycosylation could serve as a cyst‐fluid biomarker reflecting dysregulated Golgi/vesicle dynamics in IPMN progression. TLR8 glyco-down may modulate local immune surveillance, potentially influencing microenvironment interactions. Both phenomena may inform early detection or therapeutic targeting of glycosylation machinery.

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate CPD glycopeptide markers in IPMN cyst fluid and correlate with dysplastic grade.  
2. Perform site‐directed mutagenesis to assess how CPD N-glycosylation affects Golgi trafficking and protease activity.  
3. Investigate TLR8 glycosylation status in ductal epithelial and immune cells to clarify its impact on innate signaling.  
4. Extend analysis to additional glycoproteins (e.g., ADAM10, ERBB3) to map global glyco-modulatory networks in IPMNs.

References  
(none)
